ward.text: Picture a hospital ward at night. Every patient is connected to monitors.

model.text: An AI model reads their vital signs and lab results, and turns them into one number: the estimated chance of getting worse in the next twenty-four hours.

estimate.text: That number is an estimate. Not a diagnosis.

zoom.text: Now zoom out to a thousand patients, sorted by that estimated risk.

groups.text: Nine hundred of them will be fine. A hundred will deteriorate. And the two groups overlap.

thr10.text: A threshold turns the score into an action. Set it at ten percent, and everyone to the right sends an alert to the nurse.

res10.text: We catch most of the patients who will deteriorate, with about twenty false alarms.

lower.text: Now, lower the threshold to five percent.

res5.text: We catch almost everyone. But false alarms jump to around four hundred and fifty.

fatigue.text: And here is the problem. With that many alerts, people stop reacting.

missed.text: The one alert that really mattered gets swiped away with all the others. That is alert fatigue.

tradeoff.text: So there is no universal threshold. It is a trade-off between missed patients and false alarms.

depends.text: And the right balance depends on the consequences, the staff, the model, and the patient.
